newsitem.title: THAILAND: Siam Cement posts huge forex loss.
newsitem.headline: Siam Cement posts huge forex loss.

text.p: Thailand's largest industrial conglomerate, Siam Cement Plc, on Thursday announced a huge foreign exchange loss on its unhedged $4 billion foreign currency loans as a result of the baht's de facto devaluation.

Analysts said the firm's stunning losses, at a time when the country was in its worst economic slump in over a decade, would reduce its earnings per share and affect the shareholders' dividend payments.
"Siam Cement never hedged our foreign currency loans through the swap or forward contracts," its president, Chumpol Na Lamlieng, told a news conference.
"So with every one baht drop per dollar it would result in 2.4 billion baht ($84.2 million) losses in foreign exchange," Chumpol said.
Siam Cement had indirectly hedged its foreign exchange risk by borrowings in various currencies in line with the central bank's basket of currencies, he said.
Chumpol said the group's consolidated net profit could be eroded by 7.5 billion baht if the baht stood at 27.00 to the dollar and by 9.9 billion if the Thai unit eased to 30.00.
The Bank of Thailand last Wednesday scrapped the tightly controlled exchange rate regime and allowed the baht to move under a managed float system.
The baht fell by 15-20 percent following the change.
At 0400 GMT, the baht was traded at around 29.10/29.25 per dollar in the domestic market and 28.85/28.05 in the offshore market.
Chumpol said Siam Cement would record all its foreign exchange losses in the second quarter financial statements but the exact baht/dollar rate would be set later.

"If they are going to book this foreign loss of 7.5 billion baht this year (at rate of 29 baht per dollar), they will be in the red by 800 million baht," Sukhbir Khanijoh, an analyst at Thaimex Finance and Securities, told Reuters.
In 1996, the Siam Cement group posted a consolidated profit of 6.8 billion baht.
The expected loss by Siam Cement this year would reduce its earnings per share and affect the shareholders' dividend payment, Khanijoh said.
Despite the heavy losses on paper, the company's cash flow would not be affected and the company's fundamentals were still good, said another analyst at a foreign brokerage.

Chumpol said last year's cash flow generated by the company totalled 20 billion baht. He said foreign borrowings would remain a major source of funding despite baht volatility because of limited availability of long-term domestic funds.
He estimated that Siam Cement would need to raise prices of its products by five to 10 percent to reflect higher production costs resulting from the baht depreciation.
Siam Cement would also cut its investments next year by half of this year's amount of 30 billion baht due to the national economic downturn and excess production capacity, he said.
"New projects will not be considered right now because the economy remains sluggish. We also have surplus production capacity," Chumpol said.
